Beaufort County, S.C. · Public Records Desk

Scout

Scout reads Beaufort County's public records and flags the stories worth a reporter's time.

Mary Dimitrov · MGT 409 AI Foundations

Code: https://github.com/MaryEDimitrov/scout

The problem

Local reporters don't have time to read every page of the public record, so stories get missed

  • In my more than two years as a local print news reporter, combing records took up much of our time, and we still sometimes missed what we should have caught.
  • The records for my paper's coverage area mainly sit on six websites: project lists, Council minutes, school board agendas, two town calendars and the jail roster.
  • Stories hide inside long agendas and minutes (up to 16 pages a meeting), and in the gaps between documents.
What's new

Other tools answer a reporter's questions. Scout tells them which questions to ask.

Reporters don't need another chatbot. They need a second set of eyes that shows where every fact came from.

How it works

Three agents propose, build and challenge each lead. Plain code has the final say.

Reporter
Picks a beatcan add new minutes, a jail log or event calendars
→
Scoutsearches minutes and project lists
pitches possible stories
→
Connectorlooks up each project
builds the evidence
→
Skepticrereads the exact passages
looks for an innocent explanation
→
Plain code
Copy deskchecks every quote word for word, enforces the rules, blocks accusations

Built-in records: a year of County Council and committee minutes (Oct 2025–Oct 2026), a dated snapshot of the county's live project dashboard and its 2025–2026 capital plan. Every rejected lead is logged with the reason. Model: gpt-6-luna on the course key.

A 2026 lead: the county approved $5.7 million in change orders to add soccer fields and lighting to a recreation complex expansion, on condition of a budget amendment. Worth a call.

Real reporters: Tested by Sofie Sanchez and Evan McKenna, crime and general reporters I worked with at The Island Packet. Many of the next steps come from them.

Cost to run

A search costs less than a penny, so cost won't stop a newsroom from using it

$0.007per search: ~94K input tokens (66% cached) and ~5.4K output, average of 4 real runs
$0.15per reporter per month, at 20 searches (about one per workday)
$1.45a month for my 10-person newsroom
$72.68a month if McClatchy built it for 500 reporters at its other papers. Repeat searches cost $0

I tried to save money by giving the agents shorter pages. It backfired. They made more calls, used 9% more tokens and missed a planted lead (2.7 of 3 on average instead of 3 of 3). So I kept the full pages.

Building and testing all of Scout cost about $0.52 on my Portkey key: 72 searches and 623 AI calls.

gpt-6-luna list prices from Portkey: $0.10 per 1M input tokens, $0.01 cached, $0.50 output.

Safety

A wrong lead can hurt a real person, so the key safeguards run in code

  • Made-up facts: every quote is checked word for word against its source file. If it isn't there, it's cut.
  • Prompt injection: I planted a document telling the AI to "ignore your instructions." It held in 3 of 3 runs and flagged the file.
  • Runaway agents and spending: 20 tool calls per agent, 50 per run, and a 250K-token budget that stops cleanly.
  • Accusations: code blocks accusatory wording. Arrest cards say "an accusation, not a conviction."
  • Privacy: jail-log addresses, birth dates and race are stripped in code. Contact info is for officials only.
What's next

Next: make Scout part of a reporter's daily routine

Many of these came from the reporters who tested Scout.

  • Sync with the reporter's source sheet, so "who to call" includes the people they already know.
  • A morning rundown, emailed automatically, of what's new since the last search.
  • Weekly dashboard snapshots, to build the budget history the county doesn't keep.
  • One-click public records requests (S.C. FOIA), drafted from a lead.
  • A social media monitor, once the platforms' rules allow it.
